articles.title: In 2003, Mies van der Rohe's Farnsworth House went to auction as buyers considered moving it; preservation groups paid over $7.5 million to keep the Illinois landmark on its original site
articles.summary: A modernist house in Illinois came surprisingly close to being taken apart and moved away from the landscape it was designed for.
articles.body: A modernist house in Illinois came surprisingly close to being taken apart and moved away from the landscape it was designed for. In 2003, the Farnsworth House, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, was put up for sale, and some potential buyers were interested in dismantling it and moving it to another state. According to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the house faced an imminent threat, and the organisation joined Landmarks Illinois and local supporter John Bryan to save it. They bought it at auction for more than $7.5 million, keeping the landmark where Mies had intended it to stand.A house designed to blend with its surroundingsThe Farnsworth House was built for Dr. Edith Farnsworth as a weekend retreat. Mies designed the house around a simple idea: let the building and its natural surroundings become part of the same experience. Completed in 1951, the house is a 1,586-square-foot, single-storey structure made largely of steel and glass. It sits beside the Fox River in Plano, Illinois, on a 62-acre property. Instead of resting directly on the ground, the house is raised more than five feet above it, allowing floodwater to pass underneath.The design is remarkably spare. The main living area has no conventional interior walls, apart from a central service core containing the kitchen, bathrooms, fireplace and mechanical equipment. Floor-to-ceiling glass surrounds the living space, making the surrounding trees, meadow and changing seasons almost part of the interior. That simplicity became one of the reasons the house gained such importance in architectural history.From a private retreat to an architectural landmarkThe house was not without controversy. Farnsworth and Mies disagreed over the rising construction costs. What had initially been estimated at about $40,000 eventually cost more than $74,000. Their disagreement became a legal dispute, with Mies filing a lien over unpaid costs and Farnsworth countersuing. Mies won the case, although the two eventually reached a settlement.Despite the troubled relationship behind it, the building itself became increasingly influential. Its glass walls, steel frame and close relationship with the landscape came to represent the minimalist approach associated with Mies and modernist architecture. After Farnsworth eventually retired to Italy, British developer and architecture enthusiast Lord Peter Palumbo acquired the property. He restored the house and allowed limited public tours. Then came the crisis in 2003.The threat of being dismantledPalumbo put the Farnsworth House on the market, and Illinois officials were initially interested in buying it. The state later withdrew from the deal because of financial difficulties. The property was then headed for auction. That created a different kind of concern. Potential buyers were not necessarily interested in preserving the house on its original site. Several had asked about taking the structure apart and moving it elsewhere.For a building whose design depended so heavily on its relationship with the surrounding landscape, relocation would have changed something fundamental about it. The National Trust described the situation as an imminent threat to one of the most internationally significant residential designs of the 20th century.The $7.5 million rescueThe National Trust stepped in with Landmarks Illinois and local supporter and volunteer John Bryan. Together, they mounted a last-minute fundraising effort and went after the property at auction. Their winning bid was more than $7.5 million. The purchase meant the Farnsworth House would stay in Plano rather than being dismantled and shipped somewhere else. The site opened for tours in 2004, allowing the public to experience the house in the setting for which it was designed. Landmarks Illinois remains involved in preserving the property, while the National Trust operates the house.Why keeping it in place matteredThe rescue was about more than saving a famous building. The setting is an essential part of the Farnsworth House itself. Mies positioned the structure beside the Fox River and elevated it above the surrounding landscape. Its terraces, glass walls and open interior were intended to create a constant visual connection with nature. Moving the house would therefore have separated the building from an important part of its architectural idea. Today, the Farnsworth House is recognised as an iconic work of modernist architecture and has National Historic Landmark status. Visitors can still see the steel-and-glass structure beside the Fox River much as Mies conceived it.What looked in 2003 like the possible end of the house's connection to its Illinois setting instead became a major preservation success. A building that might have been dismantled was kept intact, on its original site, and opened to the public.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Residents of New York City suburbs say low-flying helicopters ferrying the ultra-rich to the Hamptons are shattering their peace on busy travel weekends.
articles.body: Residents of some leafy New York City suburbs say their peace and quiet is being shattered by helicopters ferrying even wealthier travelers out to the Hamptons, according to new reporting. Homeowners along Westchester County's Sound Shore have complained about low-flying helicopters passing over communities, including Larchmont and Mamaroneck, especially during the warmer months as the ultra rich flock to the popular eastern Long Island getaway, The Wall Street Journal recently reported. "I have to put the closed captions on so I can see what's happening on the screen," Larchmont resident Jay Davis, a Realtor and attorney, told the Journal about helicopters interrupting television and conversations at his home. AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE "I don't want to continue to live like this." Longtime resident Nancy Monzidelis told the outlet the aircraft can sound startlingly close. "One time I thought I had a helicopter in my driveway," she said. "It's not as peaceful as it was before." The dispute has created a clash between the ultra-wealthy and the not-quite-as-wealthy, the Journal noted. Larchmont and Mamaroneck homes can command seven-figure prices, according to real estate sales data. ONCE-AFFORDABLE SUMMER ESCAPE ROCKED BY SOARING COSTS AS FAMILIES SHELL OUT THOUSANDS Celebrities, including Joan Rivers, Matt Dillon and Lou Gehrig have all had ties to the two towns. The complaints highlight a growing tension surrounding one of the fastest and priciest ways to reach the Hamptons. Private helicopter services can whisk passengers between Manhattan and the Hamptons in as little as 35 minutes, compared to three hours or more by car. Some operators advertise seats starting at $795 each way, while private charters can start at more than $4,700 and unlimited summer passes can go for $25,000, according to their websites. Some residents told the Journal the helicopter traffic has been especially noticeable on summer Fridays and Sundays as travelers head east for the weekend and then return to the city. Patrick Bucquet, a Mamaroneck resident, told the outlet that helicopters can pass overhead as frequently as every 15 minutes during busy periods. "Maybe some people are doing very well, so they can afford a helicopter. Good for them," he said. FLIGHT PASSENGER'S ODD APPEARANCE AT MAJOR US AIRPORT LEADS OFFICERS TO WILD DISCOVERY "Of course, they can travel to the Hamptons," he added. "But maybe they can take another route." articles.title: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocks Panama
articles.summary: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake shook the central coast of Panama on Friday, prompting tsunami warnings for several neighboring countries.
articles.body: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake shook the central coast of Panama on Friday, prompting tsunami warnings for several neighboring countries. The earthquake hit around 1:56 p.m. ET, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Around three hours later, a second powerful earthquake measuring at 6.6 magnitude, struck Panama after a series of aftershocks, which registered magnitudes between 4.8 and 5.8, rippled across the southern tip of the country. Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt. The U.S. Tsunami Center flagged tsunami warnings for Ecuador, Colombia, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Mexico, El Salvador, Costa Rica and Peru, as well as Panama, shortly after the quake. The initial earthquake was centered about 6 miles southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama’s southern tip, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 6 miles. Tremors were also felt in the capital, Panama City, where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets. The city is known for its tall skyscrapers. Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact. “We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re OK, though we’re very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.” Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square and the Dos Continentes hotel. No casualties were immediately reported, but Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of Panama Civil Protection said injured people “have been transferred to educational centers, health centers, and hospital centers.” The province of Coclé said the governor’s palace there suffered significant structural damage, but that staff members were safely evacuated. The local government also urged community members to remain calm in the quake’s aftermath. Video aired by local news outlets showed a Catholic cathedral collapsing and part of a hotel’s facade falling onto a car in the city of Penonomé, in the central province of Coclé. Social media videos show collapsed buildings near the site of the original quake and the aftershocks, including a hotel reduced to rubble in the tourist-friendly Playa Venao. Panama’s National System for Civil Protection said it is monitoring for further reports of damage throughout the country. Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s earthquakes occur. Nearby countries sent messages of support Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.” “Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” he wrote on X. The U.S. Embassy in Panama said it was “closely monitoring” the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.

articles.title: People in Wales don't recycle at work like they do at home
articles.summary: Unclear labelling as well as a lack of recycling facilities at work or in public-facing businesses is an issue.
articles.body:
There was still "lots of room for improvement" when it comes to how much we recycle at work compared with our habits at home, according to an expert.

Figures suggest only 61% of people in Wales recycle often at their workplace, with one in five saying they do not recall seeing the appropriate facilities to do so.

Providing more bins or clearer labelling are some of the ways in which businesses could make a difference, said waste reduction charity Wrap.

But one business had already seen a "significant improvement" at their offices after removing staff's personal bins, a move that was initially met with resistance.

When recruitment firm Acorn by Synergie first moved into their offices on the outskirts of Newport in 2003, they were producing six large wheelie bins' worth of rubbish a week.

It now has just one weekly collection thanks to increased recycling, including food waste, which was their biggest adaptation, following the introduction of the Welsh government's Workplace Recycling Law in 2024.

"The main thing that we changed was removing desk bins and individual bins," said director Mark Rudge.

"We had quite a bit of resistance to that. Individuals liked having their own little waster station.

"But we put central recycling areas within each zone of the business, and eventually, people get the hang of that.

"A lot of home recycling is extremely similar, so people brought those good habits to the workplace."

Office worker Ann-Marie Derrick admitted fellow staff members had found it a pain to begin with, but it had now become "second nature".

"Anybody new coming to the office is just straight away onboard and I think we're probably quite proud as a team about how much recycling we do."

The company's environmental manager Anthony Lee said it had taken a few months for staff to fully mirror their home recycling habits at the workplace, and that there had been a "significant improvement in compliance".

Not all workers and business have adapted to the same degree.

WRAP's annual tracker survey indicated that although 94% of people in Wales say they recycle at home, only 61% do so "very often at work" with that figure dropping to below half for students at college or university.

Only 30% of respondents said they had seen lots of recycling facilities at their workplace, despite the new requirements, while 20% said they could not recall seeing any.

"It's still a relatively new thing to have recycling bins when we're away from home," said Angela Spiteri, senior marketing manager at WRAP.

"It's a very positive step in the right direction for Wales, but it's not perfect and there's a lot of things we can do to improve."

She said there was a responsibility on businesses to ensure that was possible, "providing the right bins and facilities for people to make that easier".

"I don't recycle as much when I am out and about, I just bin it," admits Gerwyn Pugh, 56, from Barry.

"It's routine [at home], but out and about every bin takes a bit more time to work out."

James Jenkins, 30, said he often took rubbish home with him given the limited options where he works.

"We only recycle cardboard because that's our only waste.

"The more industrialised businesses need to do more, because they'll have more of an impact than smaller businesses."

Natalie James, 47, said she recycled "probably about the same" at work and at home.

"Because I work at a hospital we've got the recycling categories everywhere, so we have to."

Although businesses in Wales are now required to sort their waste into six categories, collection arrangements can vary from area to area.

In the Vale of Glamorgan, businesses use a mix of council and private services, and the local authority said the change has resulted in a "higher quality of recycling".

Carys Stephens, the council's waste project officer, said there had been a "fantastic response from businesses."

"There's obviously going to be some that are critical of the idea, and they're worried about extra costs and effort that goes into segregated recycling.

"But we've been doing segregated recycling for a couple of years now, and most people just take it in their stride."

Although Wales' workplace recycling rates are "reasonably high", said consultant Rebecca Colley-Jones, "there's lots of room for improvement".

"It is a new system, so there's always a period of settling down."

She said that she was sure "we would see that 61% rise".

"Often they can be tourism or hospitality businesses, so they're having to educate their customers what to do."

Colley-Jones said individuals also needed to personally take more care.

"Our home is our castle, we're responsible for the waste and people are under a little bit of pressure, perhaps from their neighbours to look like they're recycling.

"Whereas you don't have that in the workplace.

"When people come to work, they come to work, they don't necessarily thing recycling is part of their job description.

She added: "It's trying to get people to understand that they also need to be buying into the culture of an organisation, and also the culture of Wales as a country. We are the second - best recycler in the world ."

She added that the changes had inevitably led to some costs for businesses, and varying collection arrangements can sometimes be "confusing".

Natural Resources Wales, which monitors compliance on behalf of the Welsh government, said so far no workplace had been prosecuted for failing to follow the new regulations.

A spokesperson added that 56% of businesses were found to be compliant in the first two years of the new rules, but it had provided "advice and support" and the majority of non-compliant companies "had taken steps" to address their issues.

articles.title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings
articles.summary: Tsunami warnings are issued for neighbouring countries as videos of destruction circulate online.
articles.body:
A massive magnitude 7.7 earthquake has hit Panama, damaging buildings and causing widespread shaking.

About 4.6 million people felt moderate to severe tremors as a result of the quake, according to the US Geological Survey, which has said that the effects of the quake were "likely to be widespread".

It struck just before 15:00 local time (18:00 GMT) on Friday, with an epicentre about 6.2 miles (10km) from the town of Pitaloza Arriba in south-central Panama.

Footage shared online appears to show collapsed buildings in the towns of Penonomé and Soná, including one of a man calling out to anyone trapped under the rubble of a collapsed building. No casualties have so far been reported.

Verified footage shows one side of a cathedral in Penonomé collapsed due to the shaking, as well as one of its spires.

Another video showed a local hotel had almost completely collapsed.

Ricardo Brown, who lives in the southern Herrera province, told news agency Reuters that the earthquake had damaged several homes in his neighbourhood of Las Minas.

"We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked and we're afraid it could fall on us," the 74-year-old said.

The full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, though several large aftershocks were also reported near the initial earthquake, potentially complicating the situation on the surface.

The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.

Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km from the epicentre, and were seen taking to the streets or sitting in nearby parks until the shaking had ceased.

Damage in the capital appears to be limited to that caused by debris falling from roofs.

Panama's President José Raúl Mulino said his entire government was mobilising in response to the earthquake, adding: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder."

Tsunami warnings were initially issued for 11 countries neighbouring Panama, before the US Tsunami Warning System confirmed there was no threat.

The Panama Canal - a vital waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans - was unaffected by the earthquake, the authority that oversees marine traffic through it said.

The earthquake comes just three days before Panama was scheduled to hold a national evacuation drill for dealing with a major earthquake.

It also follows devastating earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela earlier this year.

articles.title: LeBron James opened I PROMISE School in 2018, providing academic, emotional and family support; its first students are now earning college scholarships
articles.summary: LeBron James’ I PROMISE School in Akron, Ohio, opened in 2018 as part of his long-running effort to support students in his hometown.
articles.body: LeBron James’ I PROMISE School in Akron, Ohio, opened in 2018 as part of his long-running effort to support students in his hometown. Created through a partnership between the LeBron James Family Foundation and Akron Public Schools, the school was designed to provide more than classroom education, combining academic support with social-emotional resources and help for families. The school opened with 240 third- and fourth-grade students. The wider I PROMISE programme, however, began before the school, in 2011, and includes Akron students outside the school itself. In 2026, students in the programme reached an important milestone, with eligible seniors earning college scholarships to institutions including the University of Akron, Kent State University and Stark State College.I PROMISE School opened in Akron in 2018The I PROMISE School officially opened on July 30, 2018, with an inaugural group of 240 students in grades three and four. It was established through a partnership between the LeBron James Family Foundation and Akron Public Schools. The school was created to serve students identified as being behind academically and facing factors that could put them at risk of falling behind or leaving school. Its model combines traditional education with additional support intended to address challenges students may face outside the classroom. The school is a public school within Akron Public Schools, rather than a private school operated solely by James or his foundation.The I PROMISE programme started before the schoolAlthough the school opened in 2018, the broader I PROMISE initiative dates back to 2011. The LeBron James Family Foundation began working with Akron Public School students through the I PROMISE Program, providing academic assistance, incentives and support for students and their families. The programme eventually developed into a wider education initiative that included the dedicated I PROMISE School. This distinction is important because the I PROMISE School and the I PROMISE Program are not exactly the same thing. The programme includes students who attend other Akron Public Schools.Students can earn college scholarshipsJames announced a major college scholarship commitment in 2015, partnering with the University of Akron to provide eligible I PROMISE students with an opportunity to receive four-year college scholarships. The scholarships are not automatically awarded to every student who participates in the programme. Students must meet specific requirements to qualify. According to the foundation, eligible students must remain continuously enrolled in Akron Public Schools from grades three through 12, complete 120 hours of documented community service, graduate with at least a 3.0 GPA and achieve a minimum 20 ACT score.2026 brings a major milestoneThe I PROMISE programme reached another milestone in 2026, with eligible students earning scholarships to colleges including Kent State University, the University of Akron and Stark State College. The development represents the culmination of years of academic and personal support that began when many of the students were children. The foundation has also celebrated students who have already completed their university education, showing that the programme's impact now extends beyond high school graduation and college admission.First college graduates emergeIn 2026, nine I PROMISE students graduated from Kent State University and the University of Akron, according to the LeBron James Family Foundation. The graduates studied subjects including Molecular and Cellular Biology and Criminology and Justice Studies. Their graduation represents a significant step for an initiative that began with an emphasis on helping Akron students remain engaged in education. The programme has now reached the stage where students who entered its support system years ago are completing university degrees.Support continues after students reach collegeJames' initiative was designed to support students beyond simply helping them enter university. In 2016, the foundation established the I PROMISE Institute at the University of Akron. The institute provides resources and support intended to help I PROMISE students adjust to college life and remain on track towards graduation. The idea reflects the foundation's broader approach: helping students navigate academic, personal and financial challenges throughout their education rather than ending assistance when they finish high school.The programme now reaches more than 1,400 studentsThe initiative has also grown substantially since the school opened. The LeBron James Family Foundation says the broader I PROMISE programme now supports more than 1,400 students in Akron. This includes students enrolled at the I PROMISE School as well as Akron Public School students participating in the wider programme. The school itself has continued to develop its emphasis on academic achievement, STEM education, social-emotional learning and family engagement.Family support is part of the modelThe programme's approach extends beyond students' classroom performance. The I PROMISE School provides resources for families through initiatives including its Family Resource Center. The foundation has also developed the I PROMISE Village, a transitional housing programme intended to assist students and families facing housing instability and other serious challenges. The goal is to address some of the circumstances that can affect a child's education, recognising that academic success can depend on stability at home as well as what happens inside the classroom.From Akron classrooms to college degreesThe development marks a long progression for James' education initiative. The broader I PROMISE programme began in 2011, the college scholarship commitment was announced in 2015, the I PROMISE Institute followed in 2016, and the dedicated school opened in 2018. Now, in 2026, students connected to the programme are earning college scholarships while others have completed university degrees. The milestones offer a tangible measure of how James' education initiative has developed from a local programme supporting Akron schoolchildren into a long-term pathway towards higher education.You use AI every day. You can look it up." "I mean, it's interesting we're talking about this on October 7, you know, which, man, they can't even give them the one day, you know?" he said. "It's just like that the Israeli craziness. articles.title: In 2003, two brothers bought a Queens home for $850,000; after racketeering convictions and years of forfeiture litigation, the property is heading to a federal auction with bidding starting at $900,000
articles.summary: A Forest Hills home in Queens that was once owned by two brothers convicted in a major counterfeiting case is now headed for a federal auction, more than
articles.body: A Forest Hills home in Queens that was once owned by two brothers convicted in a major counterfeiting case is now headed for a federal auction, more than two decades after they bought it for $850,000. According to the US Treasury Department's auction listing, the five-bedroom property at 110-37 69th Ave. is scheduled to be sold online on October 23, with bidding starting at $900,000. The 3,572-square-foot house became entangled in federal forfeiture proceedings as authorities pursued the brothers' involvement in a racketeering conspiracy involving counterfeit US currency and money structuring.The home the brothers bought in 2003Eduard and Arkadiy Bangiyev purchased the Forest Hills property in 2003 for $850,000, using a $750,000 mortgage, according to a 2023 ruling by the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit. The house, built in 1930, sits on a roughly 5,000-square-foot lot. It has five bedrooms and 4½ bathrooms, along with an enclosed porch, finished basement, additional bedroom and bathroom, sauna and detached two-car garage.More than 20 years after the brothers purchased it, the property is being offered at a starting price only $50,000 above what they originally paid. But the house's journey from a family residence to a federally auctioned property is tied to a much larger criminal case.How the property became connected to a counterfeiting operationBeginning in 2004, the Bangiyev brothers participated in a criminal enterprise involved in manufacturing and distributing counterfeit US currency, according to federal prosecutors and court records cited by Realtor.com. The operation produced counterfeit notes in Israel and the US and moved them into the country, including shipments concealed inside containers carrying machinery. At its height, the organisation was reportedly bringing as much as $3 million in counterfeit currency into the US every three months.Federal authorities ultimately linked the operation to more than $80 million in counterfeit currency that was passed or seized around the world. The brothers were involved in financing and distributing the counterfeit money. They also operated businesses in the jewellery and gold industries, including a retail jewellery store on Long Island and later a gold-refining business in Manhattan's Diamond District. Both brothers eventually pleaded guilty in January 2015 to participating in a RICO conspiracy involving counterfeiting and money structuring.The brothers were later sentenced to federal prison, and their plea agreements also required them to forfeit property connected to or derived from their racketeering activity. The Forest Hills house later became part of the broader forfeiture dispute.The property had another complicated legal historyThe home's legal problems did not end with the counterfeiting case. According to the Fourth Circuit, a federal district court found that money used to pay off the property's mortgage and home-equity lines of credit in 2012 came from a separate scheme in which the brothers allegedly defrauded a jewellery customer of $1 million. The appellate court noted that this alleged fraud was separate from the RICO conspiracy for which the brothers were later convicted.The government had already initiated civil-forfeiture proceedings involving the Forest Hills home and another property in 2009. That earlier case was dismissed in 2011 after the brothers and their sister, Ilana Bangiyeva, agreed to a $662,500 settlement. Ownership then became the subject of another legal fight following the brothers' convictions.Years of dispute over who owned the homeBefore the convictions, the deed divided ownership among family members. Arkadiy held one-third, their sister held another third, while Eduard and his wife, Irina Alishayeva, jointly held the remaining third. Ilana argued that she had acquired interests in the home and other assets using proceeds from a gold investment she had made with her brothers. Courts rejected that argument, finding that there was not enough evidence to show the claimed investment had generated the money used to acquire the properties. A district court ultimately determined that the Forest Hills property provided a “source of influence” over the brothers' racketeering enterprise and ordered it forfeited.The government eventually obtained a two-thirds ownership interest, while Alishayeva retained one-third. There was still another hurdle. A federal judge initially allowed Alishayeva, whose primary residence was the property, to remain there for the rest of her life as long as she remained married to Eduard. That effectively prevented the government from selling its majority interest. The government challenged that decision.In 2023, the Fourth Circuit sided with the government, ruling that the lower court had exceeded its authority by preventing the government from exercising the property rights attached to its two-thirds ownership stake. The appeals court vacated that part of the forfeiture order and sent the matter back for further proceedings.Home now headed for federal auctionThe long legal battle has now brought the Forest Hills property to the auction block. The US Treasury Department is scheduled to conduct the online auction on October 23. Bidding will begin at $900,000, and prospective bidders must provide a $150,000 deposit to participate. The property is being sold “as is.” Public inspections are scheduled for October 11 and October 18 before the auction. For a home that was purchased for $850,000 in 2003, the $900,000 starting bid may appear modest compared with its current market value. But the price also reflects the unusual history attached to the property and the complicated legal proceedings that have surrounded it for years.What began as a Forest Hills family home ultimately became part of a federal forfeiture case connected to one of the larger counterfeit-currency operations investigated by US authorities. articles.body: A powerful tornado tore through a popular vacation destination Friday, overturning vehicles and damaging buildings — and leaving at least two people seriously injured. The tornado swept through Marsala, a city on the western coast of Sicily, roughly 55 miles southwest of Palermo. Dramatic footage showed the tornado swirling through the city, sending debris flying as powerful winds battered the area. TERRIFYING SCENE UNFOLDS AT SIX FLAGS AS STORM-TOPPLED TREE SENDS 4 GUESTS TO HOSPITAL The tornado overturned vehicles and seriously injured at least two people on Friday, Reuters reported. A school was also said to be damaged by the storm, along with at least one house. Damage was reported in nearby Petrosino and Mazara del Vallo, as well as Marsala. Video reviewed by Reuters also showed blown-out windows and a partially collapsed ceiling at a school in Marsala, while cars and trucks lay overturned. In addition, downed utility poles littered the streets. ISLAND GETAWAY HIT WITH URGENT WARNING AS HURRICANE DAMAGE LEAVES TRAVELERS WITHOUT POWER Salvatore Cocina, the head of Sicily's Civil Protection agency, told Reuters the scene was "almost like an American tornado." "Nothing this violent has been seen in living memory," he said. "It once again highlights the issue of extreme weather events, a characteristic of recent years due to the climate crisis," he added. articles.title: 'Thuggish' behaviour could see balaclavas banned in Newport
articles.summary: The hashtag "no face no case" has been gaining traction glorifying balaclavas as a way to avoid prosecution.
articles.body:
Balaclavas could be banned in more city centres over concerns about "thuggish" behaviour, including robberies, burglaries and drug dealing.

The social media hashtag "no face no case" has been gaining traction glorifying balaclavas as a way to avoid prosecution.

Police across the UK have said face coverings are hampering their efforts to identify potential offenders.

Officials in Newport, as well as, Coventry, Stafford and Wolverhampton, are exploring ways to strengthen existing powers to challenge those wearing balaclavas, while Nottingham has already introduced a ban.

Newport college students Luie and Nath, both 16, are supportive of a ban.

"It just looks dodgy", said Luie, "I think they should ban it. I think if you wear one you're up to no good.

"If you stop these face coverings, you'll stop crime, people can recognise you, there's CCTV everywhere, if you remove face coverings - it's a simple fix really."

"There's a lot of crime going on and they're common around the city centre," Nath added.

"I just don't think they need to wear them - bad things come with them."

"I think it's a good idea - they go around on their motorbikes intimidating people with their balaclavas on - and probably involved in crime and never get caught," said Gabrielle.

"It's quite intimidating when you're walking and they just zoom past you.

"I don't very often go into town - you feel intimidated wherever you go because there's a lot of antisocial behaviour going on.

Photographer Attela Kis, 32, is concerned about the effect it may have on people choosing to cover their faces for religious reasons.

"It depends on what type of face covering you're talking about - like a Burka for example, this is part of their religion," he said.

"When people are riding their electric bikes and committing actual crimes, it's really dangerous.

"They shouldn't cover their faces, if anyone gets hit - or anything gets stolen people need to be found and prosecuted."

Matthew Evans, one of two Newport councillors who proposed the ban, said people were wearing "intimidating" face coverings to "rob, burgle and deal drugs in our city centre" and "avoid detection".

He proposed "exemptions for religious reasons" and said this was not an "attack on the human rights of young people".

This follows a recent joint police and council crackdown, Operation Krypton, which led to hundreds of arrests.

Supt Esyr Jones from Gwent Police said 321 arrests had been made since July to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour across Newport.

Newport council said the current PSPO is due for review, "and any potential amendments can be considered as part of that process".

It said the current PSPO could potentially include face coverings, "and this too is being explored in relation to its practical implication and legalities".

But said there would be "exemptions for legitimate reasons, including religious, cultural, medical, occupational, weather or personal safety reasons".

In Nottingham, a senior police officer said offenders who wore them to hide their identity caused "substantial" problems.

Now, police there are allowed to ask people to remove their face covering if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to conceal their identity to commit crime or anti-social behaviour.

Anyone who refuses could face a £70 fixed penalty notice or face a maximum fine of £1,000.

Social media videos with the hashtag "no face no case" are used on social media, glorifying the use of balaclavas to avoid prosecution.

Last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said anti-migrant protesters covering their faces with masks and balaclavas was "not the British way."

It followed protests in Dover where demonstrators were wearing face coverings.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has called for full face coverings, including those worn for religious reasons, to be banned in public.

articles.title: Bypolls win shows deep connect with people: PM Modi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Lauding BJP's winning show in Lok Sabha and assembly bypolls as a reflection of people's \"deep-rooted connect\" with his alliance's good
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lauding BJP's winning show in Lok Sabha and assembly bypolls as a reflection of people's "deep-rooted connect" with his alliance's good governance agenda, PM Narendra Modi thanked people and said their mandate will further strengthen NDA."This mandate will give us added strength as we work for the welfare of people and to fulfil their aspirations for a brighter and more prosperous future," he said as BJP swept Nagaon Lok Sabha seat in Assam, and Nandigram and Rejinagar assembly seats in West Bengal. Its ally AINRC picked up Thattanchavady assembly seat in Puducherry.Union minister Amit Shah seized on the results coupled with NDA's win in the recent local body polls in Rajasthan and Tripura to assert that people have rejected the INDIA bloc."Despite the lies, confusion and disinformation of Rahul Gandhi and INDIA bloc, BJP is winning one poll after another under PM Modi's leadership. Having lost their support base, these parties raise questions on institutions after defeat but people have recognised their character," he said.With the win coming in the middle of street protests govt is facing from Congress and its allies besides activist groups over the SIR row, BJP trumpeted it as "democracy's resounding message to the mob".BJP's Smriti Irani said Rejinagar has 71% minority (Muslim) population. Nagaon also has a big Muslim population and had elected in 2024 a Congress MP, whose defection to BJP caused the bypoll. "While some believe in noise, these results show not only the collective wisdom of voters but also that our Constitutional framework is robust to deliver on the promise of democracy."She noted that Congress ally TVK was poised to win both assembly seats in Tamil Nadu and wondered what the main opposition party has to say about this amid its "shrill campaign" over the alleged collusion between EC and govt to help the governing alliance. articles.title: Chemists, wholesalers may need government nod to advertise prescription drugs
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Chemists, wholesalers and drug distributors may soon have to seek Centre's approval before advertising certain prescription medicines, with
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chemists, wholesalers and drug distributors may soon have to seek Centre's approval before advertising certain prescription medicines, with health ministry proposing to extend existing curbs on advertisements of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs to those involved in their sale and distribution.The proposal assumes significance as regulators have raised concerns over promotion of potent prescription medicines, including antibiotics, hormonal preparations, psychotropic drugs, anti-cancer medicines, narcotic drugs and life-saving injectables.The ministry has now proposed inserting a new sub-rule under Rule 65 of Drugs Rules, 1945, stating no advertisement of drugs specified in Schedule H, H1 or X shall be made without previous sanction of central govt. The provision would apply to those holding licences to sell, stock, exhibit, offer for sale or distribute such drugs.Importantly, the proposal does not mean that advertisements of these medicines are currently freely permitted. Drugs and Cosmetics Rules already require prior govt sanction for advertisements of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Tyreek Hill changes divorce battery trial testimony, claiming he didn't push wife but was verbally abusive
articles.summary: Tyreek Hill admitted to verbally abusing wife Lakeeta Vaccaro during intense cross-examination in their Miami-Dade County divorce battery trial.
articles.body: NFL free agent wide receiver Tyreek Hill spent his second day on the stand of his divorce battery trial admitting to verbally abusing his wife Lakeeta Vaccaro but insisting he had not harmed her physically. And through the former player's testimony on Friday, the attorneys for Vaccaro have not yet produced incontrovertible evidence of physical violence by Hill against their client. Instead, what we saw on Friday was Hill on the stand trying to erase a significant problem he created for himself the day before, while Vaccaro's attorneys pressed the issue. TYREEK HILL DENIES MOST ABUSE CLAIMS BUT ADMITS TO SHOVING WIFE INTO WALL Hill on Friday morning changed his testimony from Thursday in which he admitted to pushing Vaccaro, which caused a hole in the wall of their Sunny Isle condominium. "I told her don't you ever touch me again in your life. I pushed her against the wall. And I tried to force her to get off me," Hill testified on Thursday. "I created a hole in the wall, trying to force her to get off me that night." His testimony on Friday changed to a door caused the hole. "The door, the main door," Hill told his attorney. "I was trying to evade [Vaccaro], but I'm not trying to harm her or push her against the wall or, like, do anything crazy. As I was trying to evade, I put a hole in the wall with the door." Hill's attorneys also made sure Hill explicitly denied ever hurting his wife's breasts, which Vaccaro alleged on the stand earlier in the trial. But Vaccaro's attorneys, on cross-examination, then tried to muddy up Hill further. The plaintiff attorneys got Hill to admit he spoke in an explicitly insulting manner about his wife to her and some of his friends. "The language, I'm gonna take that all on this end, I'm not proud of that," Hill testified. "I am ashamed. I don't even go back home because my marriage failed ... The language was terrible. Was terrible. I wish I could have been better in every single moment, but I'm not perfect. "The only thing I can do is learn from it and move forward and never talk to my co-parent like that again." Vaccaro's attorneys pointed to multiple instances in which Hill's testimony Thursday contradicted statements he made during his deposition. They impeached Hill on his testimony that Vaccaro may have had something to do with a house fire at the couple's Southwest Ranches home in Broward County when, in fact, the cause was determined to be a child playing with a lighter. They attempted to impeach Hill's contention on the stand Thursday that Vaccaro was "stealing" money from the family account. They impeached Hill on his suggestion on the stand Thursday that Vaccaro had something to do with him performing worse after the marriage than before, making the point it was Tua Tagovailoa throwing the passes and coach Mike McDaniel calling the plays. "She wasn't calling the plays on the field, but at home she was calling the plays" Hill said, sticking by his guns. "If you got a real good support system at home, that's what's important." NFL PUTS 'INSPIRE CHANGE' AND 'CHOOSE LOVE' ON FIELDS BUT NOT SO AGGRESSIVE ABOUT ITS DOMESTIC ABUSE ISSUES THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Hill did, however, admit that saying Vaccaro played a role in his diminished performance was his opinion. "I'm not sitting here blaming wifey for that, bro," Hill said. "I'm not." Attorneys then impeached Hill's testimony blaming Vaccaro for Hill's mom becoming homeless. In fact, Hill moved his grandmother, which he refers to as his mom, into a hotel. Vaccaro's attorneys used video from a nanny camera inside the house to try to prove Hill emotionally hurt his wife — and Hill acknowledged that he did. "In that moment, yes," Hill agreed. "In that moment." Did Hill want to break Vaccaro mentally, Vaccaro's attorney asked? "That's not what I wanted to do, bro," Hill replied. But Hill admitted he verbally abused his wife. "When you say verbally, you mean with words, right? Hill asked. "Oh, yes sir." The trial in Miami-Dade County court is ongoing and reconvenes on Monday. articles.title: Daniel Lurie argues progressivism led San Francisco astray on public safety, drug crisis
articles.summary: Daniel Lurie says San Francisco got "entrapped in our progressive values" and got to a point where the city wasn't taking stock of their problems.
articles.body: San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said Thursday that the city had lost its way and was focused on the wrong things, arguing that the California city was "entrapped in our progressive values." "We lost our way as a city," he told CNN's Dana Bash in an interview. "We were focused on the wrong things, and today we're focused on common sense. We're focused on good governance. We're focused on delivering results for the people of San Francisco. I said from day one, public safety was going to be my number one priority. The crisis on our streets, the mental health and drug crisis is another top priority of mine. And I want to get the basics of governance right." Lurie, a moderate Democrat and heir to the Levi Strauss fortune, was elected in 2024 after defeating incumbent London Breed. "I mean, we got so entrapped in our progressive values and talking about progressivism, that we weren't taking stock of what was happening on our streets," he told Bash. "We had 810 people die of overdose in San Francisco three years ago. There's nothing progressive about that. There's nothing progressive about 30,000 car break-ins. Everyone had to deal with whether or not their car was going to be broken into," the mayor said, adding that the number of car break-ins had dropped 90%. SAN FRANCISCO STILL HASN'T RECOVERED SINCE PANDEMIC EXODUS: REPORT Bash asked Lurie about progressivism again, specifically how he defined the word. The mayor said he supported progressive values, such as taking care of the city's immigrants, and the LGBTQ+ community. "But, we got to a point where we said, 'Well, it's that person's right to be on the street using drugs,' or is that person — it's okay for someone to just go in and take what they want from a small business," he said. "In my mind, that's not progressive," Lurie continued. "There's nothing progressive about small businesses having to shutter up because they're a victim of crime over and over again. There's nothing progressive, as I said before, about 810 people dying of overdose. I'm not going to walk by somebody on the street and not do anything anymore." NEWSOM BLASTS DEMOCRATS FOR THEIR 'VICTIM MINDSET' THAT ENABLED HOMELESS CRISIS President Donald Trump praised Lurie during a cabinet meeting in March for "really trying" to improve San Francisco since taking office. "I know they have a mayor who’s trying very hard. He’s a Democrat, but he’s trying very hard," Trump said at the time. Socialism has been on the rise in the U.S., as several states have seen socialist candidates win their primary elections. In some places, progressive candidates were rejected for more moderate voices as well. Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital that even more liberal voices were calling out progressivism. "Lurie is right, and it’s not just more moderate voices like his calling this stuff out — we’ve seen AOC try to distance herself from ‘Woke 1’ as well," he said. "Some on the left have absolutely allowed themselves to get bullied into silence and, as funny and extreme a case as it was — that is how you get stories like that Massachusetts lesbian bar with the masking debacle." "Progressive policies are increasingly popular across the country, particularly on economic issues in these hard economic times," Shroff continued. "But there is also a sense that the DSA left can’t get out of its own way and can never be satisfied." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It’s not popular to say, but there is a real contingent on the left that uses these movements to center themselves and try to control others — beyond actual progressive aims," he added. "That is what Lurie is hitting on here and that is in some sense what happened in SF before his tenure. Yes, we want policies that are pro-family, pro-worker, pro-immigrant — that doesn’t mean letting the loudest voices dictate everything at the cost of a functioning city."
